employer-payroll-tax.formula: SS = min(wages, SS_base)*6.2%; Medicare = wages*1.45%; FUTA = min(wages, 7000)*FUTA_rate; SUTA = min(wages, state_base)*SUTA_rate.
employer-payroll-tax.edition: FICA - 26 USC 3101/3111 and IRS Pub 15 (Circular E), 6.2% SS / 1.45% Medicare; FUTA - 26 USC 3301-3306, $7,000 wage base, 0.6% net, IRS Form 940 - all by name.
employer-payroll-tax.freeAccess: Free at irs.gov/forms-pubs and uscode.house.gov; the SS wage base is user-supplied.
employer-payroll-tax.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
employer-payroll-tax.editionNote: The SS wage base is indexed annually (user-supplied). FUTA credit-reduction states have a rate above 0.6%. Employer pays no Additional Medicare match.

assumptions.name: Wage base
assumptions.value: the SS wage base changes yearly and is required as a user input

asymmetrical-fault-xr.formula: I_peak = sqrt(2) x I_sym x (1 + e^(-(phi + pi/2)/(X/R))), phi = atan(X/R); MF_rms = sqrt(1 + 2 e^(-2 pi/(X/R))); I_asym = I_sym x MF_rms.
asymmetrical-fault-xr.edition: First-cycle fault-asymmetry model (DC offset from X/R), an IEEE C37 / NEMA AB-4 first-cycle relation, by name; the interrupting-duty rating and coordination study govern the applied duty.
asymmetrical-fault-xr.freeAccess: The DC-offset asymmetry factors are a standard first-principles first-cycle model; X/R comes from the utility and transformer impedance data.
asymmetrical-fault-xr.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
asymmetrical-fault-xr.editionNote: First-cycle fault asymmetry model (DC offset from X/R). I_peak = sqrt(2) x I_sym x (1 + e^(-(phi + pi/2)/(X/R))) with phi = atan(X/R), the ANSI C37 / NEMA AB-1 peak that reproduces the NEMA Mp table, MF_rms = sqrt(1 + 2 e^(-2 pi/(X/R))), and I_asym_rms = I_sym x MF_rms. The first-cycle asymmetrical current, not the symmetrical RMS, is what a device's peak-withstand and a bus bracing rating must survive; the DC offset and both factors grow as X/R rises (highest near large transformers and generators, about 2.6x peak and 1.6x RMS at X/R 20-25, approaching 2.83x (2 sqrt 2) and 1.73x (sqrt 3) only as X/R grows without bound). The factors assume the worst-case fully offset phase. A design aid, not the engineer of record; the interrupting-duty rating and a protective-device coordination study govern.

assumptions.name: Peak factor
assumptions.value: I_peak/I_sym = sqrt(2)(1 + e^(-(atan(X/R) + pi/2)/(X/R))), approaching 2.828 as X/R goes to infinity

assumptions.name: RMS factor
assumptions.value: MF = sqrt(1 + 2 e^(-2 pi/(X/R))), approaching sqrt(3) in the stiff limit

assumptions.name: Worst case
assumptions.value: assumes the fully offset phase; the applied duty per the interrupting rating governs

pipe-expansion-loop.formula: Linear expansion: dL = alpha × L × dT (alpha in 1/°F). Guided-cantilever expansion loop leg: L_loop = sqrt(3 × E × D × |dL| / S_a) where E is Young's modulus (psi), D is pipe OD (in), S_a is the allowable stress (psi).
pipe-expansion-loop.edition: ASME B31.1 / B31.9 (Power and Building Services Piping) guided-cantilever method by name. Per-material alpha / E / S_a from data/plumbing/thermal-expansion-coefficients.json.
pipe-expansion-loop.freeAccess: ASME B31 series licensed; principles free in published piping-engineering texts and at most pipe-manufacturer technical pages.
pipe-expansion-loop.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed plumber / gas fitter govern. Verify against the IPC / IFGC edition adopted in your jurisdiction.
pipe-expansion-loop.editionNote: Single-edition (ASME B31 series + manufacturer alpha values; annual recheck).

assumptions.name: Coefficient table
assumptions.value: data/plumbing/thermal-expansion-coefficients.json keyed to material

assumptions.name: Allowable stress S_a
assumptions.value: engineering-practice values per material (e.g., copper 5800 psi, steel A53-B 12500 psi, PEX 1500 psi)

duct-leakage.formula: leakage_cfm = design_cfm - measured_cfm. leak_at_1inwc = leakage_cfm / (test_pressure_inwc)^0.65 (SMACNA leakage-class flow exponent). leak_per_100ft2 = leak_at_1inwc / duct_surface_ft2 × 100. Effective class = smallest SMACNA class (2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 16, 24, 48) whose limit ≥ leak_per_100ft2; above every class it reports past every class.
duct-leakage.edition: SMACNA HVAC Air Duct Leakage Test Manual (2nd ed., 2012) by name. ASHRAE 90.1-2022 (Energy Standard for Sites and Buildings Except Low-Rise Residential Buildings) §6.4.4.2.2, leakage class 4 for tested duct.
duct-leakage.freeAccess: SMACNA standards licensed; class-system overview free at smacna.org outreach. Free read-only access to ASHRAE standards at ashrae.org (Technical Resources, read-only standards).
duct-leakage.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed mechanical contractor govern. ACCA Manual J / D / S supersede rules of thumb.
duct-leakage.editionNote: The 2012 2nd edition changed the class numbers: rectangular 24/12/6 became 16/8/4 and round/flat-oval 12/6/3 became 8/4/2. Both sets are offered, and a spec written to the 1985 manual still names the old class. ASHRAE 90.1 requires class 4 for all duct.

assumptions.name: Leakage scales with P^0.65
assumptions.value: SMACNA leakage-class flow exponent

assumptions.name: Leakage classes
assumptions.value: 2 / 4 / 8 / 16 (2012) and 3 / 6 / 12 / 24 / 48 (1985) cfm per 100 ft² at 1 in WC; ASHRAE 90.1 limit is class 4
assumptions.source: SMACNA HVAC Air Duct Leakage Test Manual 2012 / ASHRAE 90.1-2022 §6.4.4.2.2

motor-operating-cost.formula: input_kW = HP x 0.746 x (load_factor/100) / (efficiency/100); annual_kWh = input_kW x run_hours; annual_cost = annual_kWh x rate. The 0.746 kW/HP is the mechanical-to-electrical conversion.
motor-operating-cost.edition: First-principles electrical-input power and the 0.746 kW-per-HP identity.
motor-operating-cost.freeAccess: First-principles physics; no licensed source required.
motor-operating-cost.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
motor-operating-cost.editionNote: Single-edition (input power and energy cost are physical relations; the 0.746 constant is a fixed unit bridge).

assumptions.name: Energy charge only
assumptions.value: the result is the energy-charge component only and excludes demand charges, time-of-use rates, and power-factor penalties
assumptions.source: utility tariff governs the full bill

assumptions.name: Efficiency basis
assumptions.value: efficiency is the full-load efficiency; partial-load efficiency differs and the load factor scales the input power linearly as a first approximation

ev-charger-load.formula: I_circuit = I_charger * 1.25 (continuous); recommended breaker = next standard size >= I_circuit; new_panel_load = existing_load + I_circuit; headroom = main - new_panel_load.
ev-charger-load.edition: NEC 2023 (NFPA 70). Article 625 (625.41/625.42 continuous-load and load-management); 220.83/220.87 panel load; 310.16 conductor.
ev-charger-load.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed electrician govern. Verify against the NEC edition adopted in your jurisdiction.
ev-charger-load.editionNote: Editions available: bundled values follow NEC 2023. NEC 2026 is the current published edition; jurisdictions on NEC 2017 / 2020 / 2023 / 2026 use slightly different ambient corrections and ampacity ranges; verify the edition adopted by your AHJ.

assumptions.name: Continuous load
assumptions.value: EVSE is a continuous load; circuit and overcurrent device are sized at 125% of nameplate

assumptions.name: Conductor estimate
assumptions.value: the recommended conductor is a first-principles ampacity estimate (copper, 75 C, 30 C ambient); verify against NEC 310.16

material-quantity.formula: Units = ceil(area / coverage per unit x (1 + waste)).
material-quantity.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.

assumptions.name: Waste factor
assumptions.value: fixed per assembly (10%; 15% for 3-tab roofing)

fire-friction.formula: FL = C × (Q/100)² × (L/100), FL in psi, Q in gpm, L in ft; C per hose diameter from NFA training tables (1.75 in, 2.5 in, 3 in, 4 in, 5 in, etc.).
fire-friction.edition: National Fire Academy hose-hydraulics training materials (U.S. government, public domain).
fire-friction.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed fire protection engineer govern.

assumptions.name: C-value table
assumptions.value: data/fire/hose-friction.json keyed to hose diameter

heat-stress.formula: NWS Heat Index = polynomial of T_db (°F) and RH (%) (Steadman regression); WBGT approximated as 0.7 Twb + 0.2 Tg + 0.1 Tdb (Twb ~ T - 30(1 - RH), Tg = T + 5, or + 15 in sun); work/rest from WBGT bands 82 / 86 / 90 F.
heat-stress.edition: NWS Heat Index polynomial by name; OSHA Heat Illness Prevention work-rest table by name.
heat-stress.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.

assumptions.name: Acclimatization
assumptions.value: not modeled

quadratic-formula.formula: ax^2 + bx + c = 0 => x = (-b +/- sqrt(b^2 - 4ac)) / (2a). Discriminant D = b^2 - 4ac signs the root type: D > 0 two real, D = 0 one real double, D < 0 complex conjugate pair. Vertex at x = -b/(2a).
quadratic-formula.edition: Classical algebra; mathematical fact. The closed form is attributed to Indian, Greek, and later Persian / European mathematicians; the modern algebraic form is universal.
quadratic-formula.governance: Estimate only. Readability formulas and similar metrics are derived from a representative population and have known edge-case noise. The classroom teacher governs final text selection, grade placement, and assessment decisions.
quadratic-formula.editionNote: Single-edition (mathematical fact). When a = 0 the tile reports a degenerate solve (linear, infinite, or no-solution per the b and c values).

assumptions.name: Coefficients
assumptions.value: all three a, b, c are real
assumptions.source: convention; complex coefficients are out of scope

earthwork-end-area.formula: Average end area V = (L/2)*(A1 + A2); prismoidal V = (L/6)*(A1 + 4*Am + A2); yd^3 = ft^3 / 27; adjusted volume = V * swell/shrink factor.
earthwork-end-area.edition: The average-end-area and prismoidal earthwork-volume methods per the FHWA and state-DOT earthwork references and FM 5-233, by name; first-principles.
earthwork-end-area.freeAccess: FM 5-233 is public-domain US Government work. Compaction swell/shrink factors are material- and spec-specific and user-supplied; the project earthwork report governs the paid quantity.
earthwork-end-area.governance: Estimate. Engineer of record governs the design and acceptance. Verify against the project structural drawings and the manufacturer's published capacity / chart.
earthwork-end-area.editionNote: Single-edition (first-principles volume methods). One material per run; cut and fill are not netted (run each separately) to avoid a sign trap.

assumptions.name: Swell/shrink factor
assumptions.value: material- and spec-specific, user-supplied

escalator-capacity.formula: steps per hour = 3600 x (speed_fpm / 60) / (step depth_in / 12); theoretical = steps per hour x persons per step; practical = theoretical x loading factor; units = ceil(design flow / practical); step load = persons per step x weight per person.
escalator-capacity.edition: The escalator theoretical-capacity relation -- steps per hour times persons per step -- and the practical loading factors published for escalator traffic design (commonly 0.5 to 0.7, with a 24 in step carrying one person and a 40 in step 1.5 to 2), by name. Throughput arithmetic, not an escalator design or a traffic study: ASME A17.1, the manufacturer, the traffic consultant, and the AHJ govern.
escalator-capacity.freeAccess: A conveyor calculation on the user's own speed, step depth, and loading assumption; no manufacturer capacity table is reproduced.
escalator-capacity.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
escalator-capacity.editionNote: An escalator's throughput is a conveyor calculation: how many steps pass a point per hour, times how many people stand on each one. Speed and step depth set the first term and step width sets the second, because a 40 inch step takes two people side by side where a 24 inch step takes one. The loading factor is what makes the answer honest, and it is the whole reason the calculation is worth running. Nobody stands on every step: riders leave a step or two between groups, they hesitate at the comb plate, and a 40 inch step often carries one person rather than two, so real observed throughput is commonly half to two thirds of the theoretical figure. The theoretical figure is nonetheless what gets quoted in a specification, and a designer who believes it specifies half the escalators the building needs -- which in a transit station means a queue that backs up onto the platform. The comparison between the two levers is the useful output. Raising the rated speed improves practical capacity in proportion and is the lever most people reach for; going from a 24 inch step to a 40 inch step at the original speed doubles it, for no change in speed and no change in the ride. Step width is the design decision and speed is a refinement. Loading factor is observational and population-dependent: commuters with luggage, shoppers with carts, and a mixed-mobility crowd all load differently.

assumptions.name: Loading factor is the honest term
assumptions.value: real throughput is commonly 0.5 to 0.7 of theoretical, and theoretical is what gets specified

assumptions.name: Width beats speed
assumptions.value: a 40 in step doubles capacity over a 24 in step at the same speed and the same ride

assumptions.name: Landings often govern first
assumptions.value: queuing and run-off space at the landings usually limits before the escalator does

hdd-pullback.formula: pullback_lb = friction_coeff x eff_weight_plf x length_ft x bend_factor + fluid_drag_lb; utilization = pullback_lb / pipe_safe_pull_lb.
hdd-pullback.edition: Simplified HDD pullback identity by name (F = mu x weight x length x bend + drag); ASTM F1962 basis, first-order form.
hdd-pullback.freeAccess: The simplified pullback identity is public first-principles friction mechanics; the full model and pipe/rig ratings come from the drilling contractor.
hdd-pullback.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
hdd-pullback.editionNote: A first-order estimate: the capstan relation (tension x e^(mu x total bend angle)) is computed beside the lumped bend factor and the larger governs; the full ASTM F1962 model's hydrokinetic drag term is not, so treat the result as a floor. The effective pipe weight already accounts for buoyancy in the drilling fluid. The drilling contractor and the rig's rated thrust govern the pull.

assumptions.name: Pullback
assumptions.value: friction x effective weight x length x bend factor, plus a hydrokinetic drag allowance

assumptions.name: Effective weight
assumptions.value: the pipe weight in the drilling fluid (buoyancy already accounted for); a ballasted or empty pipe can be near neutral

scaffold-takeoff.formula: bays = ceil(run_length_ft / bay_length_ft); frames = (bays + 1) x lifts; braces = 2 x bays x lifts; planks = bays x planks_per_bay; base_plates = (bays + 1) x 2.
scaffold-takeoff.edition: Frame-scaffold takeoff geometry by name (bays from the run, frames/braces from the bays and lifts); first-principles count arithmetic.
scaffold-takeoff.freeAccess: The takeoff is public quantity-survey geometry for a single-width frame run; the erection design comes from a competent person.
scaffold-takeoff.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
scaffold-takeoff.editionNote: The counts are for a single-width frame scaffold run. Guardrails, ties, screw jacks, and access (ladders or stair towers) are taken off separately. A competent person designs the erection.

assumptions.name: Bay layout
assumptions.value: single-width frame run, 7 ft bays default; bays = ceil(run / bay length)

assumptions.name: Components
assumptions.value: frames = (bays+1) x lifts, braces = 2 x bays x lifts, base plates = (bays+1) x 2; guardrails/ties/access separate

metal-stud-takeoff.formula: studs = ceil(wall_length_ft / (spacing_in/12)) + 1 + openings x extra_per_opening; track_lf = 2 x wall_length_ft.
metal-stud-takeoff.edition: Steel stud/track takeoff identity by name (field studs from wall over spacing, plus one and the opening allowance; track twice the wall); first-principles count arithmetic.
metal-stud-takeoff.freeAccess: The takeoff is public quantity arithmetic; the spacing and opening details come from the plans.
metal-stud-takeoff.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
metal-stud-takeoff.editionNote: Light-gauge steel framing. Extra studs go at openings (jack, king, cripple), corners, and wall intersections - entered as the opening allowance. The track is the top and bottom runners (twice the wall length). Distinct from the wood residential-framing.

assumptions.name: Spacing
assumptions.value: 16 or 24 in on center per the plans; the spacing sets the field-stud count

assumptions.name: Opening allowance
assumptions.value: extra studs per opening for jack/king/cripple plus corners and intersections (~2 each)

tree-protection-zone.formula: radius = radius_factor x DBH; area = pi x radius^2 (radius_factor 1.0 ft/in standard, 1.5 ft/in conservative/mature).
tree-protection-zone.edition: Tree protection zone / critical root zone (ANSI A300 Part 5; ISA critical root zone), by name.
tree-protection-zone.freeAccess: The one-foot-per-inch protection-radius rule is published arboricultural practice; a qualified arborist and the local ordinance govern.
tree-protection-zone.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
tree-protection-zone.editionNote: The zone is set by trunk diameter, not the canopy dripline (a narrow-crowned tree still needs the full radius, so sizing the fence to the visible canopy under-protects the roots); the standard radius is 1.0 ft per inch of DBH, with 1.5 ft per inch for mature or sensitive trees; protection is cumulative over the whole circle (fencing plus no grade change, compaction, or trenching, to the protected soil depth). A planning aid, not an arborist's prescription.

assumptions.name: Trunk-based radius
assumptions.value: radius = radius_factor x DBH, set by the trunk not the canopy; 1.0 ft/in standard, 1.5 ft/in mature

assumptions.name: Cumulative protection
assumptions.value: fencing plus no grade change, compaction, or trenching to the protected soil depth

nozzle-flow-pressure.formula: New flow = rated flow x sqrt(operating pressure / rated pressure); required pressure for a target flow = rated pressure x (target flow / rated flow)^2.
nozzle-flow-pressure.edition: Nozzle-flow square-root relation (standard spray-nozzle hydraulics), by name; USDA / land-grant extension sprayer-calibration guidance.
nozzle-flow-pressure.freeAccess: The square-root flow relation is public hydraulics. Extension calibration guidance free on land-grant university extension sites.
nozzle-flow-pressure.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
nozzle-flow-pressure.editionNote: The product label is the law (FIFRA); your state lead agency governs. Pressure is a fine-tuning lever, not a rate knob.

assumptions.name: Square-root flow law
assumptions.value: flow scales with the square root of pressure; doubling the flow needs about 4x the pressure and drives the droplets finer

assumptions.name: Flat-fan band
assumptions.value: a required pressure outside about 15 to 60 psi is flagged -- change to a different tip size instead

wire-feed-deposition.formula: Wire cross-section = pi/4 x diameter2; melt-off rate (lb/hr) = wire feed speed (in/min) x 60 x area x 0.2836 lb/in3; deposition rate = melt-off x deposition efficiency.
wire-feed-deposition.edition: Melt-off and deposition rate from wire feed speed - first-principles wire-volume geometry and steel density (0.2836 lb/in3), by name; public domain.
wire-feed-deposition.freeAccess: Pure volume-rate geometry, public; the wire feed speed, diameter, and deposition efficiency are user-supplied.
wire-feed-deposition.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
wire-feed-deposition.editionNote: First-principles wire-volume geometry and steel density. Deposition efficiency (solid wire about 0.92, FCAW about 0.85) is the deposited/melted ratio; the WPS and the process (spray vs short-circuit, gas, electrode extension) govern the real efficiency.

assumptions.name: Steel density
assumptions.value: 0.2836 lb/in3 (carbon steel), fixed

assumptions.name: Deposition efficiency
assumptions.value: deposited / melted; default 0.92 solid wire

weld-group-eccentric.formula: Two vertical welds length D, separation B: L_w = 2D; Ix = D3/6; Iy = D B2/2; J = Ix + Iy; direct shear f_d = P/L_w; torque T = P x e; f_tx = T(D/2)/J; f_ty = T(B/2)/J; resultant f_r = sqrt(f_tx2 + (f_d + f_ty)2); required leg (sixteenths) = ceil(f_r / allowable per 1/16 in).
weld-group-eccentric.edition: Eccentrically loaded fillet weld group, elastic (vector) method, per AISC 360 and the AISC Steel Construction Manual Part 8, by name.
weld-group-eccentric.freeAccess: First-principles weld-line mechanics (the elastic method); the load, eccentricity, weld geometry, and the E70 allowable (about 928 lb/in per 1/16 in, ASD) are user-supplied.
weld-group-eccentric.governance: Estimate. Engineer of record governs the design and acceptance. Verify against the project structural drawings and the manufacturer's published capacity / chart.
weld-group-eccentric.editionNote: AISC 360 / Manual Part 8 elastic (vector) method. This is the conservative elastic method (not the instantaneous-center tables), a screen; AISC edition cycles update the tabulated allowables, and the engineer of record governs the connection (then check the AISC minimum fillet for the plate thickness).

assumptions.name: Fillet allowable
assumptions.value: E70 ASD about 928 lb/in per 1/16 in of leg; editable

assumptions.name: Method
assumptions.value: elastic (vector) method, conservative vs instantaneous-center

plasma-cut-speed.formula: cut_time_min = cut_length_in / cut_speed_ipm; arc_hours_per_part = cut_time_min / 60; parts_by_pierces = floor(rated_pierces / pierces_per_part); parts_by_arc_hours = floor(rated_arc_hours / arc_hours_per_part); parts_per_set = the smaller; cost_per_part = set_cost / parts_per_set.
plasma-cut-speed.edition: Plasma consumable life from the two ratings a set carries -- pierces and arc-on hours -- with the smaller of the two governing, by name; the ratings and the cut speed for the amperage and thickness come from the torch manufacturer's published cut charts, entered rather than bundled. The manufacturer's ratings and the shop's own consumable logs govern.
plasma-cut-speed.freeAccess: The life and cost arithmetic is division on the shop's own part geometry and the manufacturer's published ratings, which the user enters.
plasma-cut-speed.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
plasma-cut-speed.editionNote: Plasma consumables wear two ways and are rated two ways. Each pierce blasts the electrode's hafnium insert, so a set carries a rated number of pierces; steady cutting erodes it more slowly, so a set also carries a rated number of arc-on hours. Which limit arrives first depends entirely on the part, because a sheet full of small holes burns pierces while a long straight rip burns hours. Reporting both and naming the governing one is what makes the calculation useful for quoting rather than merely interesting: a shop that costs consumables per pierce will underprice long cuts, a shop that costs them per hour will underprice hole-intensive ones, and across a production run the difference is real money. The two cases can sit an order of magnitude apart on the same machine in the same material, which is why a single blended consumable rate applied to every job is the wrong instrument. The parts-per-set figures are floored to whole parts, because a partial part is not a part and the set is exhausted when either limit is reached.

assumptions.name: Two ratings
assumptions.value: a set is rated in pierces AND in arc-on hours; the smaller number of parts governs

assumptions.name: Whole parts
assumptions.value: parts per set are floored; the set is exhausted when either limit is reached

assumptions.name: Cut speed
assumptions.value: from the manufacturer's cut chart for the amperage and thickness in use, entered rather than bundled

cctv-retention-days.formula: Retention days = disk_capacity_GB / (cameras * bitrate_Mbps * 0.45 * recording_hours); the algebraic inverse of the NVR storage relation (1 Mbps for 24 h = 10.8 GB/day). Recording hours = 24 continuous, or 24 * duty% for motion.
cctv-retention-days.edition: IP-video retention from available disk, camera count, bitrate, and recording hours (days = disk_GB / (cameras x bitrate x 0.45 x hours); 1 Mbps for 24 h is about 10.8 GB/day), per the standard NVR/VMS sizing practice; first-principles bitrate accounting.
cctv-retention-days.freeAccess: First-principles bitrate accounting. The H.264/H.265 bitrate estimates are scene- and vendor-specific and user-supplied; the VMS calculator and the installed cameras govern.
cctv-retention-days.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed electrician govern. Verify against the NEC edition adopted in your jurisdiction.
cctv-retention-days.editionNote: First-principles (no edition). The inverse of cctv-storage; a motion duty-cycle scales the recording hours, and the result assumes usable (post-overhead) disk capacity is entered.

assumptions.name: Bitrate
assumptions.value: per-camera bitrate is user-supplied or estimated from resolution/fps/codec

abyc-dc-wire.formula: V_drop = drop_pct/100 x system_voltage; CM = 10.75 x current x (2 x length) / V_drop; AWG = smallest standard size with circular-mil area >= CM.
abyc-dc-wire.edition: The ABYC E-11 (AC & DC Electrical Systems on Boats) DC conductor sizing by voltage drop, on the round-trip length, by name; the standard, the wire's temperature rating, and the installation govern.
abyc-dc-wire.freeAccess: The circular-mils-by-voltage-drop relation is a published ABYC E-11 method; the current, run, voltage, and allowable drop come from the circuit and the standard.
abyc-dc-wire.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
abyc-dc-wire.editionNote: ABYC E-11 DC wire sizing by voltage drop. V_drop = drop_pct/100 x system_voltage, CM = 10.75 x current x (2 x length) / V_drop, and the AWG is the smallest standard size with at least that circular-mil area. The length is DOUBLED for the round trip (out and back), unlike the NEC one-way habit. A 3% drop is required for panelboard feeders and navigation/critical loads (10% for non-critical); on a low-voltage 12 V system 3% is only 0.36 V of headroom, which drives the conductor up fast. The ABYC ampacity table, with its engine-space and bundling derates, sets a separate floor the drop size must also clear. A design aid, not the ABYC standard itself; the standard, the wire's temperature rating, and the installation govern.

assumptions.name: Round trip
assumptions.value: the length is doubled (out and back), unlike the NEC one-way habit

assumptions.name: Allowable drop
assumptions.value: 3% for panelboard feeders and critical loads, 10% for non-critical

assumptions.name: Ampacity floor
assumptions.value: the ABYC ampacity table with engine-space and bundling derates sets a separate floor

crouch-hp-for-speed.formula: hp = weight_lb x (speed_mph / C)^2, with the hull constant C ~150 average runabout-cruiser / ~190 high-speed runabout / ~210 race; the inverse of speed_mph = C / sqrt(weight / hp).
crouch-hp-for-speed.edition: Crouch's planing-speed formula (naval-architecture back-of-envelope) solved for the power, by name; the actual hull, propeller, and conditions govern.
crouch-hp-for-speed.freeAccess: Crouch's formula is a published naval-architecture estimate; the displacement, target speed, and hull constant come from the boat and its class.
crouch-hp-for-speed.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
crouch-hp-for-speed.editionNote: The horsepower Crouch's formula says a planing hull needs for a target speed, the inverse of crouch-planing-speed: hp = weight x (speed / C)^2. Because speed rises only with the square root of the power-to-weight ratio, the horsepower rises with the SQUARE of the target speed - going 40% faster needs about twice the power, and the last few mph are the most expensive. The speed is taken as miles per hour for the hull constant C; units are disputed in print: this tile treats the result as mph, as most US quotations of Crouch do, but Dave Gerr's Propeller Handbook gives the same C values with speed in knots (a 15% difference), so check which convention a C value came from (about 150 average runabout / cruiser, 190 high-speed runabout, 210 race), chosen by hull type. The formula assumes the boat is on plane; below the planing threshold it does not apply. A planning estimate, not a performance prediction; the actual hull, propeller, and conditions govern.

assumptions.name: Square-law power
assumptions.value: horsepower scales with the square of the target speed, since speed scales with sqrt(hp/weight)

assumptions.name: Units
assumptions.value: the target speed is mph, not knots; do not enter a displacement hull speed in knots

assumptions.name: Hull constant
assumptions.value: C ~150 average runabout / cruiser, ~190 high-speed runabout, ~210 race; it dominates the estimate

pulp-density-solids.formula: 1/SG_p = w/SG_s + (1 - w)/SG_l; w = SG_s (SG_p - SG_l)/(SG_p (SG_s - SG_l)); vol % = (w/SG_s)/(w/SG_s + (1 - w)/SG_l); water = Q (1 - w)/w; slurry gpm = (Q/w x 2000/60) / (SG_p x 62.428) x 1728/231.
pulp-density-solids.edition: Pulp density and percent solids by volume addition (the Marcy-scale relations, as in Wills' Mineral Processing Technology), by name.
pulp-density-solids.freeAccess: Mixture arithmetic on the user's own specific gravities and rates.
pulp-density-solids.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
pulp-density-solids.editionNote: Converts between percent solids by weight and pulp specific gravity for fully wetted solids with no entrained air, and from a dry solids rate gives the water to add and the slurry volume flow (water at 62.428 lb/ft^3). Percent solids by volume, not by weight, is what pumps and pipes see. A screen; plant sampling governs.

assumptions.name: Volume addition
assumptions.value: solids and liquid volumes add (no air, fully wetted)

power-factor-billing-savings.formula: kva_existing = real_power_kw / pf_existing; kva_target = real_power_kw / pf_target; kva_reduction = kva_existing - kva_target; kvar_needed = real_power_kw x (tan(acos(pf_existing)) - tan(acos(pf_target))); annual_usd = kva_reduction x demand_per_kva_mo x 12; payback_years = capacitor_cost > 0 ? capacitor_cost / annual_usd : null.
power-factor-billing-savings.edition: The power-triangle demand-billing method (kVA = kW / pf, correcting kVAR = kW x (tan(acos pf_old) - tan(acos pf_new)), demand savings = kVA reduction x $/kVA-month x 12), by name; the relations are public.
power-factor-billing-savings.freeAccess: The power triangle and the demand-savings arithmetic are public; capacitor-sizing and PF-billing worksheets are widely published.
power-factor-billing-savings.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
power-factor-billing-savings.editionNote: The power-triangle demand-billing method: kVA = kW / pf, correcting capacitor kVAR = kW x (tan(acos pf_old) - tan(acos pf_new)), demand savings = the kVA reduction times the $/kVA-month times twelve months. The utility rate structure governs - some bill demand directly in kVA, some in kW with a separate low-power-factor penalty clause, so the user enters the effective $/kVA-month. The kVA reduction also releases that much transformer and feeder capacity (deferring a service upgrade, a benefit beyond the demand line); harmonics and switching transients require a detuned or filtered bank the sizing here does not address. A billing estimate, not a rate-tariff analysis.

assumptions.name: Apparent power
assumptions.value: kVA = kW / power factor; correcting the power factor cuts the billed kVA

assumptions.name: Correcting kVAR
assumptions.value: kVAR = kW x (tan(acos pf_old) - tan(acos pf_new))

assumptions.name: Demand savings
assumptions.value: kVA reduction times the effective $/kVA-month over twelve months; diminishing returns above ~0.9

condenser-cop-for-heat-rejection.formula: COP = Q_evap / (THR - Q_evap), the inverse of THR = Q_evap (1 + 1/COP); W_comp = THR - Q_evap; factor = THR / Q_evap. Requires THR > Q_evap.
condenser-cop-for-heat-rejection.edition: The condenser total heat of rejection THR = Q_evap (1 + 1/COP), a standard refrigeration-cycle result, solved for the COP, by name.
condenser-cop-for-heat-rejection.freeAccess: The total-heat-of-rejection relation is a public refrigeration-cycle result; the ASHRAE Handbook covers condenser sizing.
condenser-cop-for-heat-rejection.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
condenser-cop-for-heat-rejection.editionNote: The COP implied by a measured or rated heat of rejection and the evaporator capacity, the inverse of THR = Q_evap (1 + 1/COP): the compressor work is W_comp = THR - Q_evap and COP = Q_evap / (THR - Q_evap). This reads the operating efficiency off the condenser duty and the cooling capacity; a low COP means a large heat-rejection factor (THR/Q_evap), so a struggling system overloads its own condenser and drives head pressure higher still. It uses the compressor work implied by the heat balance. A hermetic or suction-cooled compressor puts its motor heat into the refrigerant, so the measured THR includes it and the implied COP is the electrical COP; an open or belt-drive compressor rejects its motor losses to the room, so the COP implied from its THR reads high (the motor losses never reach the condenser); any desuperheater / heat-recovery split must be added back. An engineering aid; the equipment's rated heat-of-rejection data govern.

assumptions.name: Implied COP
assumptions.value: COP = Q_evap / (THR - Q_evap); requires THR > Q_evap

assumptions.name: Rejection factor
assumptions.value: THR / Q_evap = 1 + 1/COP; a low COP gives a large factor

assumptions.name: Motor heat
assumptions.value: hermetic / suction-cooled motor heat is in the THR (electrical COP); an open-drive motor rejects its losses to the room, so its implied COP reads high; no desuperheater split

duct-heat-gain.formula: U = 1/R_duct; Q = U A dT (Btu/h); dT_air = Q / (1.08 x CFM).
duct-heat-gain.edition: The conductive duct heat-gain/loss relation from the ASHRAE Handbook - Fundamentals duct-design method, by name.
duct-heat-gain.freeAccess: The Q = U A dT conduction relation and the 1.08 sensible-air constant are standard ASHRAE / duct-design values. The ductwork design and ambient conditions govern.
duct-heat-gain.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
duct-heat-gain.editionNote: The conductive duct heat gain/loss Q = U A dT with U = 1/R_duct and dT the ambient-minus-in-duct temperature (positive = the duct gains heat), and the resulting supply-air temperature change dT_air = Q / (1.08 x CFM). Doubling the duct R halves the loss (a linear return), and halving the airflow doubles the per-cfm temperature swing. This returns the steady-state conductive heat and air-temperature change: it uses a single mean dT and the R-value only, and does not model air leakage, radiant gain, or latent transfer. A design aid; the ductwork design governs.

assumptions.name: Conduction
assumptions.value: Q = U A dT, U = 1/R_duct, mean dT across the run

assumptions.name: Air-temp change
assumptions.value: dT_air = Q / (1.08 x CFM), the sensible-air constant

assumptions.name: No leakage/latent
assumptions.value: conduction only; no air leakage, radiant gain, or latent transfer

pump-specific-speed.formula: Ns = N sqrt(Q) / H^(3/4) (N rpm, Q gpm at BEP, H ft per stage); class = radial < 2,000, mixed <= 4,500, else axial.
pump-specific-speed.edition: The US pump specific speed Ns = N sqrt(Q) / H^(3/4) and the customary impeller-type bands, as compiled in the Hydraulic Institute and pump-handbook references, by name.
pump-specific-speed.freeAccess: The specific-speed definition and the impeller-type bands are public results in the standard pump references.
pump-specific-speed.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
pump-specific-speed.editionNote: The US specific speed Ns = N sqrt(Q) / H^(3/4) (rpm, gpm, ft/stage, at the best-efficiency point), and the customary impeller-type bands (radial below ~2,000, mixed ~2,000 to 4,500, axial above ~4,500) as compiled in the Hydraulic Institute and pump-handbook references. This returns the US-unit specific speed and the indicative impeller class - it uses the flow and head at the best-efficiency point per stage (divide total head by the number of stages), is the customary dimensional US form (not the dimensionless or metric nq), and does not compute the suction specific speed Nss (a separate NPSH-margin index) or select a specific pump. An engineering aid; the pump manufacturer's curves govern.

assumptions.name: Specific speed
assumptions.value: Ns = N sqrt(Q) / H^(3/4) at BEP, per stage (US dimensional form)

assumptions.name: Impeller bands
assumptions.value: radial below ~2,000, mixed flow ~2,000 to 4,500, axial above ~4,500

assumptions.name: Per stage
assumptions.value: divide total head by the number of stages before applying

column-base-plate.formula: A1_req = Pu / (0.65 x 0.85 f'c); m = (N - 0.95 d)/2; n = (B - 0.80 bf)/2; n' = sqrt(d bf)/4; l = max(m, n, n'); tp = l sqrt(2 Pu / (0.90 Fy B N)).
column-base-plate.edition: AISC Design Guide 1 §3.1 and AISC 360-22 §J8, by name; the concrete bearing uses phi_c = 0.65 with the confinement factor taken as 1.0.
column-base-plate.freeAccess: The base-plate bearing-area, cantilever, and thickness relations are published in AISC Design Guide 1 and AISC 360 §J8; the arithmetic is public.
column-base-plate.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
column-base-plate.editionNote: AISC Design Guide 1 §3.1 and AISC 360-22 §J8 concentrically-loaded column base plate: the required concrete bearing area A1_req = Pu / (phi_c x 0.85 x f'c) with phi_c = 0.65 and the confinement factor sqrt(A2/A1) taken as 1.0 (base case); the cantilever dimensions m = (N - 0.95 d)/2, n = (B - 0.80 bf)/2, and n' = sqrt(d bf)/4 (with lambda = 1.0); and the plate thickness tp = l x sqrt(2 Pu / (0.90 Fy B N)) where l = max(m, n, n'). Concentric axial compression only (no moment / uplift); the anchor rods, the shear-transfer mechanism, and the concrete breakout / pier design are separate checks. A design aid, not a substitute for the engineer of record.

assumptions.name: Bearing area
assumptions.value: A1_req = Pu / (0.65 x 0.85 f'c) with the confinement factor sqrt(A2/A1) = 1.0; a larger pier reduces the required plate

assumptions.name: Cantilever l
assumptions.value: l is the largest of m, n, and n' = sqrt(d bf)/4 (lambda = 1.0); the yield-line cantilever the plate must span

assumptions.name: Concentric only
assumptions.value: concentric axial compression; moment / uplift, the anchor rods, and concrete breakout are separate checks

contents-packout-inventory.formula: contents_volume_ft3 = floor_area_ft2 x contents_ft3_per_ft2; boxes = ceil(contents_volume_ft3 / box_volume_ft3); storage_volume_ft3 = contents_volume_ft3 x stacking_factor; truck_loads = ceil(storage_volume_ft3 / truck_volume_ft3).
contents-packout-inventory.edition: Volume-based pack-out estimating method, by name; restoration estimating practice (ANSI/IICRC S500/S700). Field-estimating arithmetic, not edition-bound.
contents-packout-inventory.freeAccess: The pack-out estimate is public estimating arithmetic; the densities are common restoration rules of thumb.
contents-packout-inventory.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
contents-packout-inventory.editionNote: Single-edition (the estimating arithmetic does not roll). The actual inventory and the box mix GOVERN; the defaults (2 ft^3/ft^2 contents, 3 ft^3 box, 1.5 stacking, 1,000 ft^3 truck) are starting rules of thumb, all editable. This is an estimating screen for the contents side of the loss. Restoration estimating practice governs.

assumptions.name: Contents density
assumptions.value: 2 ft^3 of contents per ft^2 of floor is a furnished-room rule of thumb; the actual inventory governs

assumptions.name: Stacking allowance
assumptions.value: a 1.5 factor reserves warehouse aisle and stacking space beyond the raw contents volume

soil-volume-for-canopy.formula: canopy projection area = pi/4 x the mature canopy diameter squared; soil required = that area x the entered cubic feet of usable soil per square foot of canopy; and the canopy a given pit actually supports is that relation inverted on the usable pit volume.
soil-volume-for-canopy.edition: The urban soil volume guidance by name -- commonly 1.5 to 2 cubic feet of usable soil per square foot of intended mature canopy projection. The ratio varies with species, climate, soil type, rainfall and irrigation and is ENTERED; published guidance spans a wide range and a number at the low end is not a safe default. Soil compacted for paving support is not soil roots can use, which is what the usable fraction is for. It does not design the soil or evaluate structural soil and suspended pavement systems. The urban forestry standard in use, the landscape architect, and a qualified arborist govern.
soil-volume-for-canopy.freeAccess: One area and one multiplication; no urban forestry manual is reproduced.
soil-volume-for-canopy.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
soil-volume-for-canopy.editionNote: A tree's mature size is set by the soil it has, not by the species on the plan, and canopy area goes as the SQUARE of the diameter -- so a tree meant to reach twenty five feet across needs the better part of a thousand cubic feet of soil, where a five by five pit three feet deep is seventy five. The tree does not fail: it grows to what its soil supports and stops, which is read as a species or maintenance problem years later, so the supported canopy is reported beside the requirement. Compacted soil is not soil, and the solutions -- connected trenches, structural soil, suspended pavement -- are structural rather than horticultural, which is why this belongs in the site design.

assumptions.name: The ratio is entered
assumptions.value: it varies with species, climate, soil, rainfall and irrigation
assumptions.source: the urban forestry standard in use

assumptions.name: Compacted soil does not count
assumptions.value: soil compacted for paving support is past what roots can penetrate

assumptions.name: It does not design the soil
assumptions.value: composition, drainage, aeration and rooting depth decide usability

server-inlet-envelope.formula: dew point is calculated from dry bulb and RH with the Tetens correlation, then dry bulb, RH, and dew point are checked independently against entered recommended and allowable limits.
server-inlet-envelope.edition: ASHRAE TC 9.9 thermal guidelines for data-processing environments and the Tetens saturation-vapor-pressure approximation. The current equipment-class limits govern.
server-inlet-envelope.freeAccess: The dew-point correlation is public; envelope limits are entered rather than reproducing a proprietary table.
server-inlet-envelope.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
server-inlet-envelope.editionNote: Passing dry bulb does not guarantee compliance: the hot-and-humid corner can fail the upper dew-point limit. The entered envelope must match the installed equipment class and current manufacturer requirements.

assumptions.name: One humidity limit pair
assumptions.value: the entered dew point / RH ceiling is checked for both conditions; the worked example uses the RECOMMENDED 59 F / 70% (there is no default; enter the limit), while A1 ALLOWABLE is 17 C (62.6 F) dew point and 80% RH, so enter those to judge an allowable excursion. Lower humidity limits are not checked
assumptions.source: ASHRAE TC 9.9 Thermal Guidelines, 5th ed. (2021), Table 2.1

assumptions.name: Correlation range
assumptions.value: ordinary data-center air temperatures within the validated input bounds

assumptions.name: Steady inlet condition
assumptions.value: rack-level spatial and temporal excursions are not averaged into compliance
